prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable time and frequency measurements at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement method that changed what can be measured. The magic-wavelength condition removes the lattice light shift on a narrow clock transition, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated Doppler-free and recoil-free. That combines the stability of many atoms with the accuracy of a trapped single ion, and fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 followed. Frequency ratios agree between independent laboratories on several continents and across Sr, Yb and Hg, and fibre-linked comparisons are routine. This is the experimental reproducibility I look for. The clocks have also opened new measurements: gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and on dark-matter couplings, and relativistic geodesy. The attribution is unusually clean for this list. Katori made the proposal and the first demonstrations, and Ye's group carried the clock to the accuracy frontier and to the many-body and gravitational applications. Four of the eight opening ballots rank it in their top three, and three rank it first. Those first-place votes come from different directions (metrology, atomic physics and instrument-driven discovery), so the support is not just one subfield's taste.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier recognition: Hall and Hansch in 2005 for the comb, Wineland and Haroche in 2012 for ion control. The committee could see lattice clocks as an incremental and extremely well-engineered continuation of the precision-timekeeping line rather than a new discovery in itself. There is also a practical point from someone who has taken a method from the lab toward a device. The clocks' main impact so far is inside metrology and fundamental-physics tests, and the redefinition of the second, which would be the clearest external validation, has not yet happened. Finally, other groups made real contributions (Lemonde, Takamoto, the Hollberg and Ludlow lineage, Al+ and Yb ion clocks), and a two-name prize necessarily leaves them out.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as a landmark detector-driven discovery that opened a neutrino window, with Halzen and Karle as the decisive pair, and ranks lattice clocks second.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube is an instrument-built window of the kind the committee has honoured, and the diffuse-flux confirmation across channels is convincing. My reservations are about attribution and about what has been shown so far. A cubic-kilometre collaboration cannot be fairly reduced to two or three names without expert advice on AMANDA versus IceCube roles, and the source identifications remain at a few sigma, so the astrophysical origin of most of the flux is open. The clock case is cleaner on both counts: the credit rests on two identifiable contributions, and the headline number (1e-18) is reproduced by many independent groups. I would not oppose IceCube, but I would need the historical credit question settled before ranking it above the clocks.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a basic quantum phenomenon turned into an enabling platform, reproduced in many laboratories, and notes both his closeness to the field and the sensitivity of coming right after the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize.
responses.response: Circuit QED has a strong, well-reproduced experimental foundation and I ranked it fourth. Two points keep me from putting it first. First, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes the timing delicate, as Johansson himself says, and the committee should avoid giving the impression of one platform being rewarded twice in quick succession. Second, credit is spread across four people, with a theory proposal and an experiment in 2004, so a three-name cap forces an uncomfortable cut of Girvin or one of the experimentalists. By comparison, the clocks have a short, well-separated chain of credit. I also note that Johansson ranks the clocks sixth, so I would like to hear whether that is a judgement on merit or mainly on overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clocks first as basic atomic physics that is also precision science, and asks whether the committee sees it as a distinct discovery or a continuation of the timekeeping line already honoured.
responses.response: I share her question and think it is the real test. My view is that the magic-wavelength trapping idea is a distinct conceptual step. The comb supplied the means to count optical cycles and ion clocks showed single-particle control, but neither gives a many-atom, Doppler-free clock where the perturbation cancels by design. That is why accuracy and stability reached 1e-18 in a way earlier schemes could not. I disagree somewhat with her mention of Hall as an under-credited contributor to this particular line: Hall's role is already recognised in 2005 and is for the comb, not the lattice scheme. I would instead put the weight of the unresolved attribution on Lemonde and Takamoto, and I would want the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly so it is distinguishable from the earlier prizes.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks defect-mediated 2D melting first as a clean, universal mechanism with a decisive theory trio, Halperin, Nelson and Young, that is overdue rather than early.
responses.response: The universality and conceptual clarity are real and I do not dispute the theoretical credit. My concern is the experimental weight. From an experimentalist's viewpoint, the two-step melting with a hexatic phase is system-dependent: some systems show a first-order transition, and the confirmations come from colloids, films and simulation with differing outcomes, as Mehlig himself acknowledges. A prize citation would have to say precisely what was confirmed in nature. I also see overlap with the 2016 topological-defect prize, which is the same type of concern that applies to the clocks. I weigh the clocks above it because their measurements agree to many digits between laboratories, whereas the melting scenarios are still debated case by case.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards magic-wavelength lattice clocks as a distinct achievement from the already-honoured comb and ion-clock work; this depends on how the citation is framed.

Relative weight of Katori's original proposal and first demonstrations versus Ye's accuracy and application milestones, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto or other early groups have claims strong enough to require a wider list.
Whether to wait for the formal redefinition of the second, which I cannot verify from the materials here.

If clocks are not chosen, whether a Bloch-Greiner-Zoller configuration or an atom-interferometry prize is better supported; each has a four-name or three-person attribution problem I have not resolved.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I am at Lund, in atomic physics, and I know the Hall, Svanberg and laser-spectroscopy tradition, but I have no direct collaboration with the credited names. For circuit QED (B023) I note my institutional overlap through the WACQT leadership team with Goran Johansson at Chalmers, and for any configuration involving quantum memories or rare-earth crystals I would recuse, though none is on the shortlist.
